summary:
I built SPHEREx Discovery, a web app that allows anyone to explore how the infrared sky changes over time using real observations from NASA's SPHEREx mission. For the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge, I designed the app so users can enter a sky coordinate, play observations in date order, or rapidly switch between two images to look for possible motion or changes in brightness.

SPHEREx measures different wavelengths across each image, so subtracting two exposures can make a steady object appear to change. The app aligns images by sky coordinates and checks pixel quality and wavelength overlap before subtracting or combining them. This gives students, citizen scientists, and researchers a way to investigate possible changes in NASA’s data directly in a browser, without writing code to process the original files.
details:
I built SPHEREx Discovery as a solo project for the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. It turns infrared observations from NASA/IPAC’s archive into an interactive timeline. Users can enter sky coordinates or choose a preset, replay dated observations, and rapidly alternate between two frames. I adapted the classic blink comparator used to discover Pluto so students, educators, and citizen scientists can look for signs of motion or brightness changes in a browser.

SPHEREx measures different wavelength ranges across each detector. Even two images from the same detector can make a steady source appear to change. Before subtracting or combining exposures, the app aligns pixels by sky coordinates and checks their quality flags and wavelength overlap. One test retained 207 of 225 pixels in the Epsilon Indi field, while the tested WISE 0855 pair was rejected. A separate spectral cube view shows how sky brightness varies by wavelength and marks gaps in coverage.

I used Python, FastAPI, Astropy, and NumPy to process astronomical FITS files, and React, TypeScript, and HTML Canvas to build the viewer. I added keyboard controls, tested the layout on narrow screens, and prepared a labeled cache of real observations for use during archive outages. My goal was to make the data easier to explore and help users judge which apparent changes merit follow-up.
